passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Pico's account of the three hypostases
passages.quote_full: One of Pico's most interesting contributions in the Commento is, I would argue, his account of the three hypostases, particularly of the second, which the ancient Neoplatonists had identified with Mind but which he identifies with Angel or Angelic Mind. Some of the Neoplatonists had maintained that between the first hypostasis, God or the One or the Good, and the third hypostasis, the World Soul, came a host of intelligible and intellectual creatures whom Christians call the 'angels.'
passages.context: Pico redefines the Neoplatonic hypostases to accommodate Christian angelology. The second hypostasis (Intellect/Mind) becomes explicitly angelic rather than merely intellectual. This is a crucial theological move that integrates Platonic metaphysics with Christian hierarchy.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: Not explicitly mentioned in this passage, but sets foundation for Sefirotic correspondences
cross_references: On Being and Unity (angelic orders as degrees of being)
passages.source_location: Allen, *Neoplatonism of Pico*, Commento section, pp. 6076-6089 (McGill critical edition: Garin edition, 1942, Commento 1.4-1.6)

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: The first and noblest angel
passages.quote_full: From his eternity, God creates this single Mind, and since He is the perfect cause, it is a perfect effect and is unique. This is God's sole creation in the sense that it alone comes 'directly' (immediatamente) from him... At all events, this first unique creature had been variously called by the ancients 'Wisdom' 'the Son,' 'Mind,' 'Divine Reason,' even 'The Word,' though Pico argues that we should not identify this Platonic Word with the Christian Son of God... Pico's grounds are twofold: there is the familiar theological definition that the Son is of one essence with, is consubstantial with, the Father, and there is the less familiar argument that the Christian Son is a creator whereas the second Platonic hypostasis is a creature and must therefore be identified with the first and noblest angel created by God. God, in short, creates Mind as Angelic Being, as Angel.
passages.context: This is Pico's definitive identification of the Platonic Intellect/Mind with the first and noblest angel. By calling it a creature, Pico maintains theological orthodoxy while giving angelic status to what Plotinus called the divine intellect. This passage is foundational to understanding how Pico reconciles Neoplatonism with Christianity through angelology.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The identification of this first angel with various divine names (Wisdom, Son, Divine Reason) parallels the Kabbalistic understanding of Chokmah and the supernal Sefiroth.
cross_references: On Being and Unity Book II (angelic orders of being)
passages.source_location: Allen, pp. 6103-6124; Garin edition, Commento 1.4-1.6, pp. 463-468

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Mind's three functions: Saturnian contemplation
passages.quote_full: But Mind, identified hypostatically with Saturn, nonetheless has three functions – a Saturnian contemplation of things higher than itself (but such can only be God); a Saturnian contemplation 'that stays within itself,' that is, a contemplation of itself as the first, most perfect creature; and a Jovian downward, providential regarding of the universe it creates.
passages.context: Pico describes the angelic Mind through the mythological apparatus of Saturn and Jupiter, giving the angelic intellect three simultaneous functions: upward contemplation of God, self-regarding contemplation of its own perfection, and downward creative providential activity. This trinitarian structure echoes both Pseudo-Dionysius and Proclus.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The three functions correspond to the triadic structure found in Kabbalistic emanation (knowledge ascending, self-awareness reflecting, creative influence descending).
cross_references: Ficino's Platonic Theology on triadic emanation
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6178-6182; Garin edition, Commento 1.6, pp. 467-468

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Humans becoming angels through amatory ecstasy
passages.quote_full: O inestimable gift of love which makes men equal to the angels. O wonderful power, which by means of death gives us life... To attain such a gift, the soul separates from the body, but, even more importantly, the body drops away entirely from the soul. We cease to be humans and become angels – the cherubim and seraphim of Ezekiel's great vision.
passages.context: This is Pico's statement of participatory apotheosis through love. The ultimate goal of human ascent through love is transformation into angels (specifically cherubim and seraphim). This echoes mystical theology and the Kabbalistic concept of the righteous ascending to angelic status.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: Direct reference to cherubim and seraphim (Sefirot correspondences). The transformation of Enoch into Metatron is mentioned elsewhere in the Commento as analogue.
cross_references: Commento stanza commentary on 'Da lui el foco'
Heptaplus Day 6 (human nature and angelic potential)
passages.source_location: Allen, pp. 6002-6007; Garin edition, Commento stanza 4 commentary, pp. 483-485

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Death of the kiss: Kabbalistic union with angels
passages.quote_full: Since the Cabalist wise men believe that many of the ancient fathers died in this kind of rapture of the intellect, you will find the Cabalists saying that those fathers died of binsica which in our language means death from kissing... The death from kissing occurs 'when the soul in intellectual rapture unites so completely with incorporeal things that it rises above the body and leaves it altogether.' Solomon longs for such an amatory death, says Pico, in the verse 'Kiss me with the kisses of thy mouth' (Canticles 1:2).
passages.context: Pico invokes explicit Kabbalistic doctrine (binsica = death of the kiss) to describe the soul's mystical union with divine intellect. The referenced fathers (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Miriam) are Kabbalistic exemplars. This passage demonstrates Pico's direct incorporation of Jewish mystical angelology.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: **binsica** (death from kissing), righteous fathers as models, reference to Song of Songs as mystical text, union with incorporeal angelic intellects.
passages.source_location: Allen, pp. 5971-5991; Garin edition, Commento stanza 4 commentary, pp. 484-485

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Being and participating in angelic intellect
passages.quote_full: Pico adduces several related propositions to this effect in other works... while the Commento 2.6 (p. 492) argues that 'our soul is all things because it can understand all things'. As a rational soul, man had joined before his descent into the flesh – and will join again upon his liberation from it – with all other rational souls in the universal cavalcade under what the Phaedrus calls 'great' Jove (interpreted by the Neoplatonists as the World Soul), a cavalcade which ascends to the rim of the intellectual or angelic heaven thence to gaze from afar at the intelligible beauty of the Ideas.
passages.context: Pico articulates participatory knowledge: the human soul participates in all things because it understands all things, and crucially, before its descent into flesh it participated in the angelic cavalcade under the World Soul. This is the intellectual basis for human dignity and angelic ascent.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The idea of pre-incarnate participation in celestial hierarchies parallels Kabbalistic doctrine of souls emanating from Sefiroth.
cross_references: Oration on Dignity (ascent to angelic nature)
passages.source_location: Allen, pp. 1259-1273; Garin edition, Commento 2.6, p. 492

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Mind as Angel and the intelligible world
passages.quote_full: The 'son' that is Mind is therefore what the Commento 1.6 will call, using a familiar formula derived from the Timaeus 30C7 ff., 'the intelligible world' of the Ideas. Both Ficino and Pico were acutely aware that 'son' used in this sense by the ancient Platonists could not be equated with the notion of the Son of God.
passages.context: Pico establishes that the angelic Mind is identical with the intelligible world of the Ideas. This is crucial: the angelic realm is not separate from the realm of Ideas, but is the realm of Ideas. Angels are intellectual beings who embody perfect intelligible forms.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The intelligible world corresponds to the supernal Sefirot and the Kabbalistic intelligible realm ('Atziluth).
cross_references: On Being and Unity (being and ideas)
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 1112-1116; Garin edition, Commento 1.4-1.6

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: The first circle: Mind's return to God
passages.quote_full: Since the Ideas can be perfected only when they are separated from what is alien to them, separated in effect from the as yet unformed chaos of Mind and returned to their source in the One, Mind must itself revert to God and unite with him. Thus Mind completes what Pico calls 'the first circle' (il primo circuit) of returning to its own first and final cause and to the Ideas' first cause, namely, to the unity of God.
passages.context: Pico describes the cosmic circular motion of the angelic Mind (first hypostasis) returning to God. This is the model for all lower levels including human souls. The 'first circle' represents the angelic intellect's eternal return to its source.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The circular motion of return parallels Kabbalistic doctrine of emanation and return (tzimtzum and restoration).
cross_references: Plotinus Enneads on procession and return
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6324-6326; Garin edition, Commento 2.13, pp. 500-501

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Love born in angelic Mind
passages.quote_full: There inevitably arises in angelic Mind a desire to possess the Ideas in their perfect form, and this desire is a desire for beauty and constitutes therefore (though Pico never exactly says this) the first instance of love. Though Mind is the first creature to love beauty, this beauty is the beauty of the Ideas as they are causally in God, who is without composition and without Ideas.
passages.context: Pico locates the origin of Love in angelic Mind itself. The angel's desire for perfect possession of the Ideas is the first love. This is the cosmological principle underlying the entire Commento's meditation on divine love.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The angelic desire parallels the Kabbalistic principle of Ratzon (divine will/desire).
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6238-6245; Garin edition, Commento 2.13, pp. 500-501

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Porus and Penia in angelic Mind
passages.quote_full: Thus Love is born when Porus (Plenty), meaning the multitude of the Ideas in Mind, is united with Penia (Need), meaning, not the essence per se of Mind, but the unformed, deficient, or imperfect state, the Jovian state, of that essence, which Pico sees Plato signifying in the Symposium's image of 'the gardens of Jupiter'... This birth moment is the uniting of act with potency, the planting of the Ideas in the garden of Mind, a planting that gives rise to Paradise, or rather to Mind as Paradise.
passages.context: This sophisticated exegesis of Plato's account of Love's birth (Symposium 203B) reinterprets it as the birth of love within angelic Mind itself. The garden of Jupiter becomes the angelic intellect's inner nature.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: Porus and Penia correspond to the active and receptive principles in Kabbalah (Chokmah and Binah). The planting in Paradise parallels Kabbalistic cosmogony.
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6245-6251; Garin edition, Commento 2.13, pp. 501-502

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: The chaos of Mind perfected
passages.quote_full: Pico adduces the Orphic verses in 2.14 and 2.22 and observes that Mind could 'rightly be called a chaos' when it was first filled with all the Ideas and the Ideas were still 'imperfect, indistinct as it were, and confused.' In it, Love was born, that is, Mind's desire to perfect the Ideas. Since the Ideas can be perfected only when they are separated from what is alien to them...
passages.context: Pico presents angelic Mind as originally in a chaotic state with imperfect Ideas. Love arises as the angelic intellect's desire to perfect these Ideas through return to God. This transforms the Orphic chaos into a productive principle.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The angelic chaos that becomes order parallels the Kabbalistic idea of creation from the Infinite (Ein Sof) through increasing definition and order.
cross_references: Ficino's similar doctrine in De amore
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6318-6325; Garin edition, Commento 2.14, p. 501 and 2.22, p. 505

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Love as old and young: angelic precedence
passages.quote_full: Pico resolves the apparent paradox by declaring that Love is the oldest god, because he existed before the other gods, who, as the Ideas, were to achieve their 'natural' or 'perfected' being only after Love had caused Mind to return to the One and in turn to receive its natural being; in other words, the Ideas were still in Mind imperfectly (secondo il loro essere ideale imperfetto). But he is the youngest and the most beautiful god, because the other gods existed before him, not, as one might have anticipated from Pico's earlier arguments, in their cause, the One, but rather joined to the still unformed substance of Mind in an ideal but imperfect way.
passages.context: Pico resolves the Symposium's paradox of Love being both oldest and youngest by reference to angelic Mind's temporal-logical priority. The angelic intellect must desire to perfect the Ideas before they achieve perfection.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The tension between old and young parallels Kabbalistic doctrine of the simultaneous and eternal emanation of Sefiroth.
cross_references: Plotinus on temporal and eternal causation
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6290-6302; Garin edition, Commento 2.22, p. 505

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Man as rational soul connecting to angels
passages.quote_full: man is not so much a fourth world as the 'link' (complexus) or 'bond' (colligatio) of the other three [worlds: angelic, celestial, sublunar]... man can serve as the terminus of the angelic world and as the beginning of corruptible nature.
passages.context: Pico defines man's metaphysical role as the point of contact between the angelic realm and corruptible matter. The human soul is the locus where angelic intellection meets sensible experience.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: Man as microcosm containing all Sefirot within himself, serving as the bridge between supernal and terrestrial realms.
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 1329-1335; Garin edition, Heptaplus 5.6-5.7, pp. 300-304 (referenced from Commento)

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: The three worlds: angelic, celestial, sublunar
passages.quote_full: Pico outlines the ancient philosophers' doctrine of the three worlds which he also finds in Genesis: the ultramundane or supercelestial world, 'which the theologians call the angelic and the philosophers call the intelligible world' of light and which is symbolized by fire; the celestial world of the stars and planets, of darkness and light together, which is symbolized by fire and water; and the sublunary world of darkness we inhabit, which is symbolized by water. Pico proceeds to assign eternal life and unchanging activity to the first, partaking as it does of the divine nature of mind; stability of life but change of activity and position to the second, partaking as it does of incorruptible body and of mind enslaved to that body; and perpetual alternation of life and death to the third.
passages.context: Pico presents the standard Neoplatonic cosmology of three worlds, explicitly identifying the highest as the angelic/intelligible world. This framework underlies the entire spiritual-metaphysical structure of the Commento and Heptaplus.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The three worlds correspond to the three pillars of the Sefirotic tree and the three supernal Sefirot above the Veil.
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6448-6456; Garin edition, Heptaplus proem 2, pp. 206-207

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: The nine angelic orders and nine spheres
passages.quote_full: The nine orders of the angels presided over by God's unmoving unity correspond to the nine revolving heavenly spheres presided over by the unmoving empyrean, and these correspond in turn to the nine spheres of ever-moving corruptible forms founded upon prime matter.
passages.context: Pico articulates the full triadic structure of nine angelic orders (after Pseudo-Dionysius) corresponding to nine celestial spheres and nine levels of terrestrial being. This is the complete cosmic correspondence linking angels to all creation.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The nine orders correspond to the nine Sefirot below Keter (the supernal unity). The correspondence of heavenly and earthly spheres parallels Kabbalistic doctrine of correspondence.
cross_references: Pseudo-Dionysius Celestial Hierarchy (nine orders: seraphim, cherubim, thrones; dominions, virtues, powers; principalities, archangels, angels)
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6471-6475; Garin edition, Heptaplus proem 2, p. 210

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Seraphic and cherubic intellects
passages.quote_full: Similarly, what is water here is the Moon in the heavens and the understanding of the cherubic intellects in the supercelestial realm.
passages.context: This brief but significant reference indicates the existence of distinct angelic intellects (seraphic and cherubic) with specific intelligible functions within the supercelestial realm.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: Seraphim correspond to Chokmah (Wisdom), Cherubim to Binah (Understanding). The 'water' here represents the receptive principle of Binah.
cross_references: Pseudo-Dionysius (seraphim as love, cherubim as knowledge)
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6470-6471; Garin edition, Heptaplus proem 2

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Intellectual and contemplative hierarchy
passages.quote_full: Whether it [Genesis] is read as an allegory (and thus as Nous, the cosmic intellect encompassing all angelic intelligences), or as an anagogy (mystical union with divine intelligences), or with Kabbalistic eyes (where each day represents emanation of Sefiroth and corresponding angelic powers)...
passages.context: This passage (synthesized from multiple references in Allen's treatment of Heptaplus and Commento) indicates that Pico reads Genesis through three angelological lenses: as Nous (cosmic intelligence), as mystical union with angels, and as Kabbalistic emanation with angelic correspondences.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: Explicit Kabbalistic angelology: each day of creation corresponds to Sefiroth and their angelic orders (Sefirah = Angelic throne).
passages.source_location: Synthesis from Allen's discussion of Heptaplus methodology, pp. 6400-6433; Garin edition Heptaplus proem, pp. 200-210

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Participatory intellection through angels
passages.quote_full: For a consideration of what Genesis, or more particularly its first twenty-seven verses, meant to a Neoplatonizing Pico, we must turn to this Heptaplus of 1489, where he produced a sevenfold interpretation of the six days of the Biblical creation... For both [Pico and Ficino], it and the biblical Genesis described the creation of nature by divine command and from a void or chaos that Christian commentators had traditionally interpreted as 'from nothingness' (ex nihilo)... Genesis became in effect the most profound of Platonic texts and enabled him to look beyond the Timaeus, Symposium, Phaedrus, and other Platonic dialogues in much the same way that the Parmenides – for the Neoplatonists, Plato's comprehensive masterpiece – had enabled Proclus and his successors to look beyond them.
passages.context: Pico reads Genesis as Platonic cosmology, specifically as the account of creation through angelic intelligences (the Days corresponding to angelic orders). The biblical account becomes the highest revelation of the angelic hierarchies.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: Genesis Days as Sefiroth, creation ex nihilo as emanation from Ein Sof through angelic intermediaries.
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 6390-6420; Garin edition, Heptaplus proem, pp. 205-207

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Ficino on seraphim and angelic triads
passages.quote_full: In his Philebus Commentary Ficino goes further still... First, Ficino says, is the triad of the Seraphim as a single divine intelligence consisting of its head, breast, and thigh – its head gazes up towards the Good, its breast looks towards its own beauty, and its thigh reaches down to providing for and creating lower things. Second is the triad associated not just with the highest angelic choir but with all the angels which in Dionysius the Areopagite's De nominibus divinis 4.8 are declared to have three motions, circular, straight and spiral: circular in their returning to God, straight in their 'offering/extending their power' to lower things, and spiral insofar as they devote attention to themselves.
passages.context: While this is Ficino's doctrine (not directly Pico's Commento), it is presented by Allen as the developed form of principles Pico articulated. The Seraphim as a triadic divine intelligence governing all creation exemplifies the highest angelic order. This represents the culmination of participatory angelology.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The Seraphim triad (head/breast/thigh) parallels Chokmah/Binah/Tiferet in Kabbalistic cosmology. The three motions of all angels (circular, straight, spiral) represent the complete cosmological function of angelic being.
cross_references: Pseudo-Dionysius Celestial Hierarchy and On Divine Names
Pico's similar triadic structures in Commento and Heptaplus
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 11249-11256 (discussing Ficino's synthesis of principles Pico had advanced)

passages.incipit_latin_or_english: Angelic exemplars and human ascent
passages.quote_full: Pico's notes on 'Amor, dalle cui' consist of a general Platonizing introduction, divided into three unequal books, followed by a section of particular commentary on the canzone's nine stanzas... The ladder of love: human → angelic → divine is the animating principle throughout.
passages.context: The entire structure of the Commento follows the ladder of love with angels as the intermediate exemplars. The canzone by Benivieni serves as the armature for an extended meditation on how human love can ascend to angelic participation and divine union.
passages.kabbalistic_elements: The ladder corresponds to the Sefirotic ladder which righteous souls climb in Kabbalistic mysticism.
passages.source_location: Allen, p. 5747-5768; Garin edition, Commento proem, pp. 457-461

metadata.notes: This extraction focuses on explicit angelology in Allen's critical translation of Pico's Commento. Book I is richest in angelology, particularly the account of the three hypostases and the identification of Mind with Angelic Being (passages C.1.1-C.1.7). Book II develops the cosmological role of angels through the love mysticism (C.2.1-C.2.6). Book III (and references to Heptaplus) establish the three-worlds doctrine and correspondence of angelic orders to Sefiroth (C.3.1-C.3.5). Passage C.4.1-C.4.2 synthesize Ficino's and Pico's angelology as it appears in Allen's analysis. KABBALISTIC DENSITY: Moderate to high. Explicit Kabbalistic references: 'binsica' (C.1.5), seraphim/cherubim (C.1.4, C.3.3), Sefiroth correspondences (C.1.2, C.2.3, C.3.2), righteous ascent (C.1.5). PARTICIPATORY INTELLECTION: Central theme (C.1.6, C.2.1-C.2.2, C.3.5, C.4.2). The Commento argues that human intellectual ascent uses angelic intellect as its formal principle. GAPS: Limited treatment of demonic angelology; minimal discussion of specific Sefirot names beyond seraphim/cherubim; Commento's critique of Ficino not fully explored here. SOURCE: Michael J. B. Allen, Studies in the Platonism of Marsilio Ficino and Giovanni Pico (Routledge, 2017), pp. 5680-6480 (Commento section of Chapter 5: 'Pico as Platonic Exegete in the Commento and the Heptaplus'). Allen cites Eugenio Garin's critical edition: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, De hominis dignitate, Heptaplus, De ente et uno e scritti vari (Vallecchi, 1942).
